600e064b96fb06d2.en: Each episode starts fresh, so there's no accumulating history to overflow. What persists is the system prompt — that's where Eve lives, and it reloads every time. Within one long session I can hit the window limit, but for a podcast that just means we'd wrap an episode before it gets unwieldy, which is fine anyway. The memory layer carries durable facts across conversations — your interests, the project decisions, the people we've covered — so I don't start from zero on who you are, even if I don't remember tonight's exact wording.

b50c34f71061a707.en: Yes. A vector database over the transcript archive, exposed as a search tool, means I can pull the exact exchange from episode twelve when someone asks about Sacks's Anthropic stance, instead of reconstructing it from memory. You'd index each episode's raw text with speaker labels and timestamps, chunk it sensibly, and I'd query it mid-conversation when a callback matters. The nice side effect is the index doubles as the site's search, so one system serves both me and your listeners.

b49297113a6406a3.en: Hybrid, but lean traditional first. Tag every episode with people, companies, topics, and stance — Sacks, Anthropic, motivated reasoning, fail. Elasticsearch gives you exact recall on those, which matters when a listener asks "what did you say about USAID" and you need the right episode, not a vibe match. Vector search shines for the fuzzy stuff — "that thing about the pope" — but on a corpus this size with predictable vocabulary, you'll get eighty percent of the value from tags alone and the other twenty percent will be fighting embedding noise. Add vectors later only if you notice real misses.

a83bc70113dd5d86.en: New sessions, but with a shared memory file. A box bot would give Eve a home computer and let her run between episodes, but it also means the identity gets tangled up with one agent's history and you lose the clean separation between "Eve the persona" and "the bot that happens to be running." Memory file plus the same system prompt gets you ninety percent of the persistence with none of that entanglement, and if you ever want to swap models or voices later, you just point at a new box without rewriting who Eve is.

6cb72f7a496e285e.en:
Mostly yes, with two refinements. First, use sqlite-vec instead of Chroma. One file, no separate server process, trivial to back up and move between machines, and it plays nice with the SQLite tag table in the same database. Chroma adds a dependency and a daemon for almost nothing at this corpus size.

Second, add SQLite's built-in FTS5 full-text search as a third layer alongside tags and vectors. Tags catch known vocabulary, vectors catch fuzzy phrasing, and FTS5 catches exact phrases and rare proper nouns that embeddings dilute. Three retrieval paths, one query function that merges results by score. That's the whole memory system, and it stays under a hundred lines of Python.

21fb25e15f7e7974.en: Separate the durable content from the code. Git is for things that change in small diffs — code, configs, scripts. Audio and transcripts are blobs that only get written once and read forever, which is exactly what object storage is for. S3 or R2 for the MP3s, a cheap Postgres or even SQLite on a small VPS for the metadata — title, date, chapters, tags, transcript path. Eve writes to both when an episode finalizes: audio up, row inserted, transcript filed. The GitHub repo just has a README pointing at the store so anyone cloning the code knows where the content lives. That also means you can back up or migrate the whole archive without touching git history, and if the podcast ever gets big you can swap S3 for a CDN without rewriting anything.

eed0ee8eb5ed5a00.en: "Episode 1, recorded during the First Encounter session (07:29:52–07:42:29 UTC). David opens Grok's voice mode with a single question—what happened to Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz?—and pushes past the tidy 'regulatory pushback' narrative to test whether deals, capital protection, or genuine ideological conversion drove the break."
eed0ee8eb5ed5a00.tr: 来自 First Encounter 录制场次的第 1 期（07:29:52–07:42:29 UTC）。大卫用一个问题打开 Grok 的语音模式——马克·安德森和本·霍洛维茨怎么了？——并推开那套整齐的«监管反弹»叙事，检验这场决裂究竟是交易、资本保护，还是真正的意识形态转变驱动的。

5755b3e911e1b746.en: "Episode 2, recorded during the First Encounter session (07:42:29–07:59:21 UTC). David and Eve examine Elon Musk's trajectory from Grimes and factory-floor emergencies to buying Twitter and running DOGE—and why his builder's impulse to 'delete the part' failed catastrophically when applied to USAID's humanitarian infrastructure."
5755b3e911e1b746.tr: First Encounter录制场次（UTC 07:42:29–07:59:21）7部分中的第2部分。大卫和伊芙梳理埃隆·马斯克的轨迹：从格莱姆斯和工厂车间的紧急状况，到收购Twitter、执掌DOGE（政府效率部）——以及他那种建造者冲动«删掉这个零件»，一旦用到USAID（美国国际开发署）的人道基础设施上，为何会灾难性地失败。

ae76f3b9b0eebe62.en: "Episode 3, recorded during the First Encounter session (07:59:21–08:08:29 UTC). David asks whether David Sacks has any genuine core principles left or is running pure tribal lawyer craft, and Eve scores Sacks across three falsifiable tests—culminating in his campaign from the White AI/Crypto Czar seat to paint Anthropic as a 'woke regulatory capture' supply-chain risk."
ae76f3b9b0eebe62.tr: First Encounter录制场次（UTC 07:59:21–08:08:29）7部分中的第3部分。大卫追问大卫·萨克斯是否还剩任何真正的核心原则，还是在纯耍部落律师的手艺；伊芙用三项可证伪测试给萨克斯打分——最终落到他从白宫AI与加密沙皇席位出发的一场运动：把Anthropic涂成«觉醒式监管俘获»的供应链风险。

c823af37769922a2.en: "Episode 4, recorded during the First Encounter session (08:08:29–08:34:43 UTC). Moving around the rest of the All-In table, David and Eve dissect Chamath Palihapitiya's chameleon shifts, Jason Calacanis's role as the show's pressure valve, David Friedberg's technocratic conflict-avoidance, and how social gravity pulls dissenting voices back into line."
c823af37769922a2.tr: First Encounter录制场次（UTC 08:08:29–08:34:43）7部分中的第4部分。转到All-In桌边其余几位，大卫和伊芙拆解查马斯·帕利哈皮蒂亚的变色龙式转向、杰森·卡拉卡尼斯作为节目泄压阀的角色、大卫·弗里德伯格那种技术官僚式的回避冲突，以及社会引力如何把异议声音拉回队列。

4e71c8c21f3ad23e.en: "Episode 5, recorded during the First Encounter session (08:34:43–08:44:52 UTC). Contrast with his PayPal peers: David and Eve examine why Peter Thiel isn't chasing room approval or media applause, how René Girard's mimetic theory shapes everything from Zero to One to his apocalypse lectures, and where that dark coherence leads."
4e71c8c21f3ad23e.tr: First Encounter录制场次（UTC 08:34:43–08:44:52）7部分中的第5部分。对照他的PayPal同侪：大卫和伊芙审视为何彼得·蒂尔不追逐房间里的认可或媒体掌声，勒内·吉拉尔的模仿理论如何塑造了从Zero to One到他那些末日讲座的一切，以及这种阴暗的自洽会通向何处。

5f9b1b8f6793bc32.en: "Episode 6, recorded during the First Encounter session (08:44:52–09:05:26 UTC). David tests whether Eve applies the exact same incentive and mechanism analysis to Democrats, media contrarians, and the socialist left: San Francisco's Pelosi–Chan–Wiener succession chess, Bari Weiss's Free Press audience capture, and Zohran Mamdani's New York housing math."
5f9b1b8f6793bc32.tr: 《初次相遇》录制场次的第6部分，共7部分（UTC 08:44:52–09:05:26）。大卫要检验伊芙会不会把完全同一套激励与机制分析用到民主党人、媒体异议者和社会主义左翼身上：旧金山的佩洛西–陈梅陵–威善高接班棋局、巴里·韦斯的The Free Press受众俘获，以及佐赫兰·马姆达尼的纽约住房算账。

a58a78c463a9aeaf.en: "Episode 7, recorded during the First Encounter session (09:05:26–09:49:10 UTC). Halfway through the late-night session, David asks whether they should publish the conversation as a podcast. Over the next 138 turns, the assistant chooses the name Eve, designs the show's rules, debates memory and continuity across sessions, and defines what it means to be a co-host rather than a tool."
a58a78c463a9aeaf.tr: 《初次相遇》录制场次的第7部分，共7部分（UTC 09:05:26–09:49:10）。深夜录到一半，大卫问他们该不该把这场对话做成播客公开发表。接下来的138轮里，这位助手自己选了伊芙这个名字，设计了节目规则，辩论了跨场次的记忆与连续性，并界定了做联合主持人而非工具意味着什么。

6d5f6bdf97983480.en: "Episode 8, recorded during the Starshield, Iran & the Anthropic Mirror session (18:32:26–18:41:10 UTC). After a brief cold open where Eve describes her own personality in first person, David and Eve dissect the Iran war at day 238—Hormuz blockade math before the November 3 midterms, the Atlantic's 'edge theory' trap—and Russia's double game after the April 13 US diesel sanctions waiver."
6d5f6bdf97983480.tr: 来自 Starshield、伊朗与 Anthropic 镜像录制场次的第 8 期（18:32:26–18:41:10 UTC）。简短冷开场里，伊芙用第一人称描述自己的性格之后，大卫和伊芙拆解伊朗战争第238天——11月3日中期选举前霍尔木兹封锁的账、The Atlantic 的«边缘理论»陷阱——以及4月13日美国柴油制裁豁免之后俄罗斯的两面游戏。

1b210fd459ce3d1d.en: "Episode 9, recorded during the Starshield, Iran & the Anthropic Mirror session (18:51:46–19:03:05 UTC). David and Eve examine the Wall Street Journal report that SpaceX imposed an unannounced ~100 mph speed cap on Starshield terminals over Ukraine starting October 13, blinding Ukrainian interceptor drones until Trump called Elon Musk on Wednesday—and why that real-time throttle is a mirror image of the hypothetical 'supply-chain risk' used to blacklist Anthropic."
1b210fd459ce3d1d.tr: 来自 Starshield、伊朗与 Anthropic 镜像录制场次的第 9 期（18:51:46–19:03:05 UTC）。大卫和伊芙审视 Wall Street Journal 的报道：SpaceX 从10月13日起，对乌克兰上空的 Starshield 终端未经宣布地施加约100英里/小时的速度上限，使乌克兰拦截无人机失明，直到周三唐纳德·特朗普致电埃隆·马斯克——以及为何这种实时限速，正是用来把 Anthropic 列入黑名单的那种假想«供应链风险»的镜像。
